title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 108
paragraphs: When day dawned, the Greeks, seeing that the land-army was still in place, supposed the fleet was still at Phaleron as well; and thinking they would fight another sea-battle, they prepared to repel it. But when they learned that the ships had departed, they at once decided to pursue them. They pursued as far as Andros, but caught no sight of Xerxes's fleet; and when they reached Andros, they deliberated what to do. Themistocles expressed the opinion that they should take their course through the islands and pursue the ships, afterwards sailing straight to the Hellespont to break up the bridges. But Eurybiades expressed the opposite view, saying that if they broke up the floating bridges, they would do Greece the greatest possible harm. For if the Persian were cut off and compelled to remain in Europe, he would try not to remain still, since if he stayed still, none of his affairs could advance, no way back to his country would appear, and his army would perish of hunger. Whereas if he pressed on, all Europe might go over to him city by city, nation by nation — the inhabitants either conquered or surrendering on terms before they were conquered; and he would have for food the Greeks' crops growing year by year. On the other hand (Eurybiades thought), a Persian defeated in the sea-fight would not stay in Europe, and so he should be allowed to flee until in his flight he reached his own land. Then afterwards they could begin the contest for the land that belonged to the Persian. The other Peloponnesian commanders adhered to this opinion as well.
